analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2017 tax law's individual rate cuts, child credit, and estate tax exemption permanent.
analysis.headline: The House bill to make the 2017 tax law's individual tax cuts permanent was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on January 3, 2025 and has had no further action; 53 House Republicans cosponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: Key parts of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, including the lower individual tax rates, the bigger standard deduction, and the $2,000 child tax credit, were written to expire after 2025. This bill would make them permanent, along with the 20% deduction for business owners who file through pass-through firms, a doubled estate tax exemption, and larger alternative minimum tax exemptions. It would also make permanent some limits added in 2017, like the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes, and would permanently repeal the personal exemption and the tax break for employer-reimbursed bicycle commuting [S2]. The bill went to the House tax-writing committee and has not moved since [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Middle-income families would keep the lower tax rates, the larger standard deduction, and the $2,000 child credit. Owners of pass-through businesses (profits taxed on owners' personal returns) would keep a deduction worth 20% of business income. The largest dollar gains would go to high earners and wealthy estates: the 37% top rate, expanded minimum-tax exemptions, a capital gains-rate threshold raised above $425,000-$479,000, and a $10 million base estate and gift tax exemption (about $20 million per couple) would all become permanent [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families, business owners, and wealthy estates

how_it_helps.text: Keeps the seven individual tax rates set in 2017, including the 37% top rate, from reverting to higher pre-2017 rates after 2025 [S2] [S3].
Makes the $2,000 child tax credit, the $2,000-plus standard deduction increase, and the larger alternative minimum tax exemptions permanent [S2].
Keeps a 20% deduction for income from pass-through businesses (income taxed on owners' personal returns), which is scheduled to expire [S2] [S3].
Doubles the base estate and gift tax exemption to $10 million and makes it permanent, so fewer large estates pay estate tax [S2] [S3].
Permanently excludes from income student loans forgiven when a borrower dies or becomes totally and permanently disabled, including private student loans [S2] [S3].
Expands tax-free 529 education savings withdrawals to homeschooling and K-12 expenses like tutoring, testing fees, and educational therapies [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government collects less revenue, which means larger deficits unless spending is cut or other taxes are raised. Households in high-tax states keep the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes permanently. Families who itemize lose the personal exemption permanently. Bicycle commuters lose the exclusion for employer-reimbursed bike commuting, and workers other than active-duty military lose the moving-expense deduction and exclusion [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The largest dollar benefits go to the highest earners and heirs of large estates, while a permanent extension adds to federal deficits; the revenue cost falls on future taxpayers generally [S2].

The bill locks in the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes and the $750,000 limit on mortgage-interest deductions, raising taxes for itemizers in high-tax states and expensive housing markets relative to pre-2017 law [S2] [S3].
It permanently repeals the personal exemption, which especially affects families with several dependents who itemize, in exchange for a larger standard deduction and child credit [S2] [S3].

The child credit remains largely nonrefundable and phases out above $200,000-$400,000 of income, and the bill repeals later-enacted credit expansions, so the lowest-income families get less from it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Most working households would see real tax savings from permanence, and avoiding a sudden tax increase in 2026 is a genuine benefit. But the bill's design is skewed: the provisions worth the most per dollar — the estate tax doubling, the expanded minimum-tax exemption, the raised capital gains threshold, and the pass-through deduction — concentrate gains at the top, and the whole package is deficit-financed with no offsetting revenue. It also locks in limits, like the $10,000 state and local tax cap, that many families view as a tax increase. The cost of permanence is never paid for in the bill itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on day one of the new Congress, and the committee has not taken it up, so it sits with no vote scheduled while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Vern Buchanan introduced the TCJA Permanency Act on January 3, 2025, the first day of the 119th Congress [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action since [S5].
53 House Republicans, all members of the sponsor's party, signed on as cosponsors [S4].

The bill would make permanent the expiring individual provisions of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, including rates, the standard deduction, the child tax credit, the pass-through deduction, and the doubled estate tax exemption [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so no one has gained or lost; current law, under which the individual tax cuts are still scheduled to expire after 2025, remains in place while the bill waits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; current law still stands

for.name: Rep. Vern Buchanan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 3, 2025 to make the 2017 tax law's individual provisions permanent

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 3, 2025 and has not scheduled a markup or advanced it

sides.party_line_note: All 54 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support listed; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is visible only in the sponsorship list.

industries.note: The bill makes permanent the 20% qualified business income deduction, a benefit that flows to owners of businesses taxed on personal returns and skews toward higher-income owners. The cost shows up as forgone federal revenue rather than as a payment by the people who use the deduction.

The permanent 37% top rate, higher alternative minimum tax exemption, capital gains rate threshold raised above roughly $425,000-$479,000, and the doubled $10 million estate and gift tax exemption concentrate the largest benefits at the top. Forgone estate and income tax revenue is a cost borne by the treasury and future taxpayers.

industries.industry: Private K-12 schools, tutors, and education service providers
industries.note: The bill permanently expands 529 savings accounts to pay tax-free for K-12 private school tuition, tutoring, testing, and educational therapies, routing public tax benefits through private education providers. This creates a permanent tax-advantaged customer base for private schools and education vendors alongside the public school system.

Making the $10,000 cap on the state and local tax deduction permanent reduces the federal tax value of state and local taxes for residents, which high-tax states and their taxpayers have pressed to lift. The bill locks the cap in place rather than easing it.

The bill makes permanent the 60%-of-income limit on deductible cash contributions but also repeals the overall limit on itemized deductions, changes that pull in opposite directions for large donors and the charities they fund.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since referral, standalone bills like this typically die quietly in committee. Because the 2017 individual tax cuts are scheduled to expire after 2025, this material is more likely to move as part of a larger tax package, such as a budget reconciliation bill, than on its own; if that does not happen, the bill's provisions lapse with the Congress at the end of 2026.
